descripcion: At C2 the caution stack is calibrated so precisely that the choice of a single hedge word signals a specific point on the certainty scale to an expert reader: may suggests genuine doubt, would appear to signals strong but not absolute confidence, cannot be ruled out signals a low but non-zero probability worth flagging.

filas: flags a risk worth naming, not expecting
near-conclusion, stops short of stating fact
raises a possibility while minimising commitment
cuadroReferencia.notaPie: These distinctions matter most to expert readers in a field; a general reader may not register the difference, which is exactly why the choice signals expertise.

ejemplos.texto: A confounding variable cannot be ruled out at this stage.
The results would appear to support the original hypothesis.
It is not inconceivable that the effect is seasonal rather than causal.

notas: Cannot be ruled out is weaker than is possible — it flags that something hasn't been excluded, without suggesting it's likely.
Would appear to sits just below a confident claim; dropping would appear to and stating the fact directly would overclaim.
It is not inconceivable that is a deliberately understated way to raise a possibility that the writer actually considers worth taking seriously.

es.en: Spanish academic writing hedges with fewer distinct lexical grades and relies more on the conditional («podría no descartarse») to cover several nuances at once. Spanish speakers at C2 tend to collapse the fine English scale into two or three options, losing the exact signal of certainty an expert reader expects.
es.es: El español académico utiliza menos grados léxicos distintos para atenuar y confía más en el condicional («podría no descartarse») para cubrir varios matices a la vez. Los hispanohablantes de C2 tienden a reducir la fina escala inglesa a dos o tres opciones, perdiendo la señal exacta de certeza que espera un lector experto.

de.en: German academic writing traditionally hedges less explicitly than English and relies on «Konjunktiv II» and a few particles («dürfte, wohl») rather than a finely graded set of lexical hedges. German speakers therefore tend to reduce the English scale to might and may, or to under-hedge claims that an expert English reader expects to see qualified.
de.de: Deutsche wissenschaftliche Texte schwächen traditionell weniger ausdrücklich ab als englische und verlassen sich eher auf Konjunktiv II und wenige Partikeln («dürfte», «wohl») als auf eine fein abgestufte Reihe lexikalischer «hedges». Deutschsprachige reduzieren die englische Skala daher oft auf «might» und «may» oder formulieren Behauptungen zu direkt, die ein englischer Fachexperte abgeschwächt erwarten würde.

it.en: Italian academic prose hedges with the conditional, and «sembrerebbe» or «parrebbe» correspond closely to it would appear. Italian speakers therefore have one precise point of the scale ready, but tend to overuse conditional forms (it would be possible that…) where English would choose a lighter lexical hedge.
it.it: La prosa accademica italiana attenua con il condizionale, e «sembrerebbe» o «parrebbe» corrispondono bene a «it would appear». Gli italofoni hanno quindi già un punto preciso della scala, ma tendono a sovrausare il condizionale («it would be possible that…») dove l'inglese sceglierebbe un hedge lessicale più leggero.

fr.en: French academic prose hedges with the «conditionnel» and impersonal forms («il semblerait que, on pourrait penser que»). The typical calque is one could think that, which sounds stilted in English, and the tendency to express every nuance with the conditional rather than with the English range of lexical hedges.
fr.fr: La prose académique française atténue avec le conditionnel et des formes impersonnelles («il semblerait que», «on pourrait penser que»). Le calque typique est «one could think that», raide en anglais, ainsi que la tendance à exprimer chaque nuance par le conditionnel au lieu d'utiliser toute l'échelle lexicale anglaise des «hedges».

pt.en: European Portuguese often hedges with the future («poderá indicar, será que»…), and the calque will indicate sounds far too certain in English. «Parece» corresponds well to appears, but Portuguese speakers need the full English scale between may and would appear.
pt.pt: O português europeu frequentemente atenua com o futuro («poderá indicar», «será que…»), e o calque «will indicate» soa certo demais em inglês. «Parece» corresponde bem a «appears», mas falantes de português precisam dominar toda a escala inglesa entre «may» e «would appear».

errores: Using a stronger hedge than the evidence actually supports, or vice versa.
Treating cannot be ruled out and is possible as interchangeable, when they signal different degrees of expected likelihood.
Dropping would appear to and overclaiming a near-conclusion as established fact.

autochequeo: Does each hedge match the actual level of certainty the evidence supports?
Have I distinguished cannot be ruled out from is possible in intent?
Does would appear to stop short of overclaiming?
Would an expert reader in this field read the precise level of confidence I intend?
Is there at least one flat, unhedged claim to show the contrast?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the precision of the hedging scale. Check whether each hedge word matches the intended level of certainty, not just whether a hedge is present. Do not rewrite the text.

es: «*no se puede descartar*» rendered as *cannot be discarded* instead of *cannot be ruled out*.
de: «*nicht auszuschliessen*» rendered as *not to exclude* instead of *cannot be ruled out*.
it: «*non si può escludere*» rendered as *cannot be excluded*, which reads as non-native, instead of *cannot be ruled out*.
fr: «*on ne peut exclure*» rendered as *one cannot exclude* instead of *it cannot be ruled out*.
pt: «*não se pode descartar*» rendered as *cannot be discarded* instead of *cannot be ruled out*.
